ranking.rationale: Personal income is one of the strongest and most state-stable predictors of health insurance coverage because eligibility, affordability, and access to employer-sponsored plans depend heavily on earnings. It captures broad socioeconomic capacity without directly encoding geography, and has larger marginal predictive value than demographic or race-related shortcuts.

Employment status is a strong, broadly state-stable determinant of health insurance coverage beyond income, capturing access to employer-sponsored insurance and labor-force attachment without directly encoding geography. It adds major marginal signal complementary to personal income and is less brittle for OOD generalization than race, ancestry, migration, or state identifiers.

Age is one of the most stable predictors of health insurance coverage across states because eligibility and coverage mechanisms vary strongly over the life course, including dependence for children, labor-market attachment for working ages, and near-universal Medicare eligibility at older ages. It adds major signal beyond income and employment while being less likely than race, ancestry, citizenship, or state to encode brittle geographic or demographic shortcuts.

Education adds strong, broadly state-stable signal for health insurance coverage beyond income, employment, and age because it captures job quality, benefits access, and socioeconomic resources. It is more semantically portable across states than race, ancestry, migration, or state code, and has wider relevance than child-specific or narrow disability variables.

Citizenship status adds strong, broadly state-stable signal for health insurance coverage beyond income, employment, age, and education, because eligibility and take-up differ systematically for citizens vs noncitizens across the US. It is more semantically tied to coverage mechanisms than race, ancestry, mobility, or geography, and less redundant than nativity given the finer-grained categories.

Disability status is strongly and semantically linked to health insurance coverage through Medicare/Medicaid eligibility, work limitations, and healthcare need. It adds stable signal beyond income, employment, age, education, and citizenship, and is less likely than race, ancestry, sex, or state to act mainly as a brittle geographic or demographic shortcut.

Nativity adds stable signal for health-insurance eligibility and coverage patterns beyond citizenship, income, employment, age, education, and disability. It captures broad foreign-born vs native-born differences that generalize across states better than race, sex, mobility, or geography-coded features, while avoiding the direct domain leakage of state.

Hearing difficulty adds health-related functional limitation signal that is directly relevant to insurance need and eligibility, and it should transfer more stably across states than race, ancestry, migration, or geography features. It also complements existing disability, age, employment, and income features with less shortcut risk than demographic identity variables.

Cognitive difficulty is a strong, semantically stable correlate of health insurance need and eligibility across states, adding health-status signal beyond income, employment, age, citizenship, nativity, and hearing difficulty. It is less likely than race, sex, ancestry, migration, or state to act as a brittle geographic or demographic shortcut.

Military service status adds stable signal for health insurance because veterans and active-duty-related populations have distinctive, broadly consistent coverage pathways nationwide. It is less geography-specific and less likely to act as a brittle demographic shortcut than race, ancestry, or state, while offering complementary information beyond income, employment, age, education, citizenship, nativity, and disability.

Marital status adds broadly stable signal for health insurance coverage through spouse/dependent eligibility and household attachment, complementing income, employment, age, education, citizenship, and disability without directly encoding geography. It is more semantically portable across states than race, ancestry, migration, or state identifiers, and more broadly useful than child-specific or narrower impairment variables.

Vision difficulty adds health-related functional limitation signal that is plausibly linked to insurance coverage and healthcare engagement across states, while being less geography-specific and less likely than race/ancestry or state code to act as a brittle demographic shortcut. It also complements the already selected disability and hearing/cognitive difficulty features with relatively stable marginal information.

White race indicator adds meaningful residual signal for health-insurance coverage through broadly stable structural disparities in access and employer-sponsored coverage, while being less geography-specific than ancestry or migration and more generally useful than niche indicators with small support. It complements income, employment, education, citizenship, nativity, age, marital status, and disability without directly encoding state.

Sex adds broad, state-stable signal for health insurance coverage through labor-market attachment, spousal/dependent coverage patterns, and pregnancy-related eligibility, while being less geography-specific and less brittle than ancestry, mobility, or state identifiers; it also complements already selected income, employment, age, marital status, and disability features with low redundancy.

Recent childbirth adds stable signal for health insurance through pregnancy, postpartum, and dependent-coverage pathways that generalize across states. It is less geographically brittle than migration or ancestry variables, more broadly useful than parent-employment status, and avoids directly encoding the train/test domain like state.

ESP adds household-context signal that is plausibly relevant to insurance coverage, especially for children and dependents, and is more semantically stable across states than geography or fine-grained ancestry/race indicators. The remaining race dummies are partly redundant with already selected RACWHT and risk demographic shortcutting, MIG can encode state-specific mobility patterns, ANC is brittle and culturally/geographically entangled, and ST directly leaks domain.

Recent mobility status can add stable signal for health insurance coverage through life transitions, job changes, and administrative continuity, while remaining less geography-specific than state code and less likely than detailed race/ancestry indicators to act mainly as demographic shortcuts already partly captured by income, employment, citizenship, nativity, age, and marital status.

Asian race indicator adds useful residual signal for health-insurance coverage beyond income, employment, age, education, citizenship, nativity, disability, sex, and white-race status. It is more semantically tied to persistent differences in eligibility, employer coverage, and immigrant-family composition than ancestry, while being less directly geographic and less brittle than state code. Among remaining race indicators, it likely offers the strongest broad, nonredundant signal because white status is already included and Asian populations have distinctive coverage patterns not captured by the selected features.

Adds a broad race-related signal that can still matter for insurance coverage disparities, while being less geography-specific and less brittle than ancestry or state. It likely contributes more stable marginal value than the very small race categories, and with only white and Asian indicators already present, this fills an important remaining gap.

Black race indicator adds remaining broad, nationally stable signal about health-insurance disparities beyond income, employment, citizenship, disability, nativity, education, sex, and white/Asian/AIAN indicators. It is more semantically tied to structural access differences than ancestry, less sparse and brittle than NH/PI indicators, and safer for OOD generalization than state code.

Adds residual race/ethnicity information not covered by the already selected race indicators and can capture stable disparities in insurance access better than ancestry; more semantically tied to coverage than ANC, while avoiding the clear geography leakage of state and likely lower-yield, smaller-population race indicators.

Adds a small amount of individual-level demographic signal beyond the existing race indicators, while remaining more stable across states than ancestry and far less harmful than explicit state code. It is likely weak but still the best remaining marginal feature for health-insurance prediction after income, employment, age, education, citizenship, disability, nativity, sex, marital status, and major race indicators are already included.

Adds a small amount of individual-level health-insurance signal via race/ethnicity disparities while avoiding the severe OOD leakage of state code and being less geography-tied and redundant than ancestry, especially given multiple race indicators are already included.

Ancestry may add a small amount of stable signal about immigration background, language/cultural context, and family structure beyond nativity, citizenship, race, and Hispanic origin, while state code is a direct geography/domain indicator that is highly likely to hurt out-of-distribution generalization by encoding state-specific policy and distributional artifacts.

Only remaining candidate. However, it should be strongly downweighted in any feature-importance prior because state directly encodes the domain and is unlikely to provide stable out-of-distribution signal beyond geography-specific policy and market differences.

llm_calls.content: {"selected_feature_id":10,"rationale":"Nativity adds stable signal for health-insurance eligibility and coverage patterns beyond citizenship, income, employment, age, education, and disability. It captures broad foreign-born vs native-born differences that generalize across states better than race, sex, mobility, or geography-coded features, while avoiding the direct domain leakage of state."}

{"selected_feature_id":11,"rationale":"Hearing difficulty adds health-related functional limitation signal that is directly relevant to insurance need and eligibility, and it should transfer more stably across states than race, ancestry, migration, or geography features. It also complements existing disability, age, employment, and income features with less shortcut risk than demographic identity variables."}

{"selected_feature_id":13,"rationale":"Cognitive difficulty is a strong, semantically stable correlate of health insurance need and eligibility across states, adding health-status signal beyond income, employment, age, citizenship, nativity, and hearing difficulty. It is less likely than race, sex, ancestry, migration, or state to act as a brittle geographic or demographic shortcut."}

{"selected_feature_id":8,"rationale":"Military service status adds stable signal for health insurance because veterans and active-duty-related populations have distinctive, broadly consistent coverage pathways nationwide. It is less geography-specific and less likely to act as a brittle demographic shortcut than race, ancestry, or state, while offering complementary information beyond income, employment, age, education, citizenship, nativity, and disability."}

{"selected_feature_id":2,"rationale":"Marital status adds broadly stable signal for health insurance coverage through spouse/dependent eligibility and household attachment, complementing income, employment, age, education, citizenship, and disability without directly encoding geography. It is more semantically portable across states than race, ancestry, migration, or state identifiers, and more broadly useful than child-specific or narrower impairment variables."}

{"selected_feature_id":12,"rationale":"Vision difficulty adds health-related functional limitation signal that is plausibly linked to insurance coverage and healthcare engagement across states, while being less geography-specific and less likely than race/ancestry or state code to act as a brittle demographic shortcut. It also complements the already selected disability and hearing/cognitive difficulty features with relatively stable marginal information."}

{"selected_feature_id":20,"rationale":"White race indicator adds meaningful residual signal for health-insurance coverage through broadly stable structural disparities in access and employer-sponsored coverage, while being less geography-specific than ancestry or migration and more generally useful than niche indicators with small support. It complements income, employment, education, citizenship, nativity, age, marital status, and disability without directly encoding state."}

{"selected_feature_id":3,"rationale":"Sex adds broad, state-stable signal for health insurance coverage through labor-market attachment, spousal/dependent coverage patterns, and pregnancy-related eligibility, while being less geography-specific and less brittle than ancestry, mobility, or state identifiers; it also complements already selected income, employment, age, marital status, and disability features with low redundancy."}

{"selected_feature_id":24,"rationale":"Recent childbirth adds stable signal for health insurance through pregnancy, postpartum, and dependent-coverage pathways that generalize across states.
